items.title: Your heart pumps 7000 litres of blood every day
items.claim: Resting heart rate ~70 bpm. Stroke volume ~70 ml. Cardiac output ~5 litres per minute, 7200 litres per day. Over an average lifetime: 250 million litres pumped — enough to fill 100 Olympic swimming pools.
items.prompt: How can such a small muscle pump so much?

options.text: The heart is hollow so volume doesn't matter

Continuous high turnover: each heartbeat moves a small volume, but ~100,000 beats per day add up; cardiac muscle is uniquely adapted (intercalated discs, dense mitochondria, near-zero anaerobic capacity) to never tire
Most of the volume is recycled within the heart
Blood is much lighter than water

items.reveal:
Cardiac muscle (myocardium) is structurally distinct from skeletal muscle. Cells are short, branching, with one or two nuclei, joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions that synchronise contraction.

About 30% of cardiac muscle volume is mitochondria (vs 1-2% in skeletal muscle). The heart oxidises fatty acids preferentially and never fatigues under normal conditions.

It's also self-rhythmic: the sinoatrial node (in the right atrium) generates 70-80 spontaneous depolarisations per minute, propagated via the AV node and Purkinje fibres. Cut all nerves to the heart and it keeps beating (just at a different rate).

Under exercise, cardiac output can rise to 25+ L/min (5x resting) — by increasing both heart rate and stroke volume. Elite athletes have larger left ventricles and lower resting heart rates (40s, even 30s).

The heart's own coronary arteries feed it. Block one and the muscle downstream dies in minutes — myocardial infarction.
items.why: Continuous lifelong pumping sounds impossible. Heart muscle isn't ordinary muscle — it's a specialised contractile tissue evolved precisely never to stop.

items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.

options.text: Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.

items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.
